subsection: 9. Practical application of two methods of preservation

notes.b: Home freezing works best with fresh, good-quality food that is frozen soon after it is harvested or bought.
points: Vegetables that freeze well include carrots, peas, beans and broccoli.
Fruit that freezes well includes apples and strawberries.
Meat and fish, baked foods, soups, sauces and complete meals can all be frozen at home.
Bananas and lettuce do not freeze well and are not suitable for home freezing.
Melons and pears also freeze poorly.

notes.h: Home freezing: preparing and blanching vegetables
points: 1. Wash the vegetables and prepare them by trimming, peeling and cutting them into even pieces.
2. Blanch by plunging the pieces into boiling water for the recommended time for that vegetable.
3. Cool quickly by transferring the pieces to ice-cold water for the same time as the blanching.
4. Drain thoroughly and dry the pieces on absorbent paper or a clean tea towel, so that surface water does not form ice.
1. Cool cooked food completely before packing, because warm food raises the temperature of the freezer.
2. Open-freeze fruit such as strawberries by spreading them in a single layer on a tray, so the pieces do not stick together.
3. Pack the food in usable, family-sized portions in strong, moisture- and vapour-proof freezer bags or rigid containers.
4. Leave headspace in rigid containers, because liquids expand on freezing.
5. Remove the air from bags and seal them securely with ties or heat sealing.
6. Label each pack with its contents and the date.
Switch the freezer to its fast-freeze setting 3–4 hours before adding food.
Add no more than one-tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24-hour period.
Place the packs against the sides or base of the freezer so that they freeze quickly.
Store the frozen food at -18°C or colder.
Use knives, graters and food processors carefully, cutting away from the body and keeping fingers clear of the blades.
Wash hands before preparation, cover any cuts with a dressing, and tie back long hair.
Use oven gloves when handling the blanching pan, turn pan handles inward, and do not overfill the pan.
Avoid overloaded sockets, trailing flexes and wet hands near electrical appliances.
Keep raw and cooked foods separate during preparation and clean surfaces between tasks.

notes.h: Home jam making: suitable fruit and ingredients
points: Use ripe, sound fruit that is free from mould and bruising.
Pectin is found mainly in the skin and core of fruit; cooking apples, blackcurrants and citrus fruit are high in pectin.
Strawberries are low in pectin, so lemon juice or another acid is added to help the jam set.
The sugar is measured in the correct proportion for the fruit and warmed, then stirred in until fully dissolved before the mixture is boiled.
1. Wash the jars and lids, sterilise them, and keep them hot until filling.
2. Wash the fruit, remove stalks and damaged parts, and cut the fruit as the recipe requires.
3. Simmer the fruit gently in a heavy-based pan until it softens and releases its pectin.
4. Add the warmed sugar and stir until it has completely dissolved.
5. Boil the mixture rapidly until setting point is reached.
6. Test for setting point with a cold saucer, pushing a drop of jam with a finger to see if it wrinkles, or with a sugar thermometer.
7. Skim off the scum from the surface, then pour the jam into the hot jars and leave a small space at the top.

notes.h: Home jam making: packaging and storage
points: Use clean, undamaged glass jars with new lids, and wipe the rim of each jar before sealing.
Seal each jar immediately while the jam is hot, so that a vacuum forms as it cools.
Label each jar with the contents and the date.
Store sealed jars in a cool, dry, dark place, and refrigerate any jar once it has been opened.
Hot sugar syrup can cause severe scalds, so handle the pan with oven gloves and pour carefully.
Do not overfill the pan, as the mixture foams up and boils over when it is at a rolling boil.
Keep children and pets away from the cooker while the jam is boiling.
Remove scum with a clean, dry spoon, because a wet or used spoon can introduce micro-organisms into the jam.

keyTerms.definition: Plunging vegetables into boiling water for a short time to inactivate enzymes before freezing, then cooling them quickly in ice-cold water.
Freezing food in a single layer on a tray before packing, so the pieces do not stick together.
The empty space left at the top of a container so that liquid can expand on freezing without breaking the container.
Using the freezer's fast-freeze setting to freeze food quickly so that small ice crystals form.
A natural substance in fruit that forms a gel with sugar and acid to set jam.
The stage in boiling jam at which enough water has evaporated and the mixture forms a gel when cooled.
Removing the scum that rises to the surface of jam during boiling.
To destroy micro-organisms on equipment, such as jars and lids, by boiling or heating them.

factCards.term: Temperature for fast-freezing food at home
factCards.definition: About -25°C, which freezes food quickly so that small ice crystals form.
Boil them in water, cool them in ice-cold water for the same time, then drain and dry them.

factCards.term: Four guidelines for freezing fresh food
factCards.definition: Cool the food first; freeze no more than one-tenth of the freezer capacity in 24 hours; use airtight, labelled packaging with the air removed; allow room for liquids to expand.
The pieces stay separate, so they can be packed in usable portions, and they freeze quickly in a single layer.
Fruit, sugar and an acid such as lemon juice.
The cold saucer test and the sugar thermometer test.
Cooking apples, blackcurrants and citrus fruit.

questions.prompt: Explain why vegetables are blanched and then plunged into ice-cold water before they are packed for the freezer.
questions.model: Blanching heats the vegetables in boiling water to inactivate enzymes, which would otherwise cause loss of colour, flavour, texture and nutrients during frozen storage. Plunging them into ice-cold water for the same time stops the cooking, so the vegetables stay firm and do not become overcooked. Drying them removes surface water, which would otherwise form ice and encourage the growth of micro-organisms.

questions.prompt: Describe a home-made preserve from fruit, from choosing the ingredients to storing the finished product, with the safety precautions at each stage.
questions.model: Ingredients: ripe, sound fruit; for a low-pectin fruit such as strawberries, lemon juice or another acid is added; sugar in the correct proportion. Preparation: wash and sterilise jars and lids and keep them hot; wash and prepare the fruit. Cooking: simmer the fruit gently in a heavy-based pan to soften it and release pectin; add the warmed sugar and stir until dissolved; boil rapidly to setting point, tested with a cold saucer or sugar thermometer. Safety: use oven gloves, turn pan handles inward, do not overfill the pan, keep children away from the cooker and handle hot syrup carefully. Finishing: skim the scum with a clean, dry spoon, pour into hot jars leaving a small space at the top, wipe the rim, and seal immediately so a vacuum forms as the jar cools. Storage: label with contents and date and store in a cool, dry, dark place; refrigerate once opened and discard any jar with a bulging lid, gas, mould or off-odour.
